![](data:image/png;base64,)A green composite hydrogel based on cellulose and clay as efficient absorbent of colored organic effluent

Qiyang Wang[a](#_bookmark0),[b](#_bookmark1), Yixiang Wang[a](#_bookmark0), Lingyun Chen[a](#_bookmark0),[⁎](#_bookmark2)

a _Department of Agricultural, Food and Nutritional Science, University of Alberta, Edmonton, T6G 2P5, Canada_

b _School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Anhui University, Hefei 230601, China_

A R T I C L E I N F O

_Keywords:_ Cellulose/MTM hydrogel Adsorption kinetic Methylene blue

Kinetic model

A B S T R A C T

This work has developed a convenient way of constructing wood cellulose and clay green composite hydrogel as efficient adsorbent of colored organic effluent. The optimized cellulose/montmorillonite(MTM) hydrogels showed excellent methylene blue (MB) absorption with the maximum capacity of adsorption (Qmax) of 277 mg/ g, which is not only higher than MTM alone, but also higher than many other natural clay composite adsorbents. Adsorption mechanism and kinetic studies that the physisorption was a major processing in MB absorption and the adsorption mainly occurred in the internal structure of composite hydrogel. This indicated that the MTM embedded inside played the most critical role for the MB dye adsorption. Owing to its biodegradability and excellent adsorption capacity, cellulose/MTM hydrogel has good potential for colored organic effluent treat-ment. The simple procedure and cost effective wood cellulose as raw material for the composite absorbent construction presented in this research are favorable for industrial applications.

# Introduction

There are increasing concerns of the colored organic effluent dis-charged to the environment, which is causing serious water, soil pol-lution and health problem. Giving azo dye as an example, their dis-charge into the environment has caused damage of human liver and the central nervous system ([Demirbas, 2009](#_bookmark28); [Greenstein, 2016](#_bookmark33); [İyim &](#_bookmark39) [Güçlü, 2009](#_bookmark39); [Kyzas, Siafaka, Pavlidou, Chrissafis, & Bikiaris, 2015](#_bookmark41); [Lin](#_bookmark44) [& Juang, 2002](#_bookmark44)). Both chemical and physical methods have been applied to remove organic effluent from industrial wasterwater such as ion exchange, solvent extraction, biological treatment, flotation and ad-sorption ([Babel & Kurniawan, 2003](#_bookmark16); [Crini, 2006](#_bookmark25); [Ilangovan et al., 2017](#_bookmark38); [Lodha & Chaudhari, 2007](#_bookmark48); [Parshetti, Chowdhury, & Balasubramanian,](#_bookmark54) [2014](#_bookmark54); [Puanngam & Unob, 2008](#_bookmark55); [Zouboulis, Matis, & Stalidis, 1992](#_bookmark63)). Among these methods, adsorption has been considered as an efficient and economic process. So far, some materials such as activated carbon, metal organic framework (MOF) and carbon nanotubes have been studied as adsorbents, and their adsorption, kinetics, and mechanisms have been reported ([Al-Ghouti et al., 2010](#_bookmark12); [Haque, Jun, & Jhung, 2011](#_bookmark36); [Hasar, 2003](#_bookmark37); [Li et al., 2003](#_bookmark43); [Liu & Lee, 2014](#_bookmark46); [Ma, Cui, Dai, & Li, 2011](#_bookmark49)). However, Effective and economic adsorbants with good handling properties are still required, especially those based on natural products because of their renewable and biodegradability.

Sodium montmorillonite (MTM) is a naturally generated host-guest

layered materials consisting of 2:1 layered silicate, which is composed by one aluminum octahedral layer between two silicate tetrahedral layers ([Chen, Zhou, Cao, Xue, & Lu, 2014](#_bookmark24); [Sinha Ray & Okamoto,](#_bookmark56) [2003](#_bookmark56)). Sodium montmorillonite is an interesting adsorbent material to treat organic effluent owing to its high surface area due to layered structure, mechanical and chemical stability, and cation exchange ca-pacity. However, it is very difficult to remove the sodium montmor-illonite from water system, causing secondary pollution to the en-vironment. To solve this problem, clays have been combined with polymer materials. For example, nanoclay composite hydrogels with polyethylene glycol and poly acrylic acid were developed for congo red and methyl violet removal from waste water. Such composite systems combine the advantage of polymer materials as superabsorbent and the nanoclay for synthetic dye adsorption ([Bhattacharyya & Ray, 2015](#_bookmark17)). More recently combining MTM with renewable biomass macro-molecules such as cellulose and chitin is gaining increasing attention to creat biodegradable systems ([Bhattacharyya & Ray, 2015](#_bookmark17); [Gong, Wang,](#_bookmark32) [Tian, Zheng, & Chen, 2014](#_bookmark32); [Kissinger, Fix, & Rees, 2007](#_bookmark40); [Wang, Wang,](#_bookmark61) [Chen, Cai, & Zhang, 2017](#_bookmark61)).

Wood cellulose is an abundant raw material from hardwood, soft-wood, and agricultural residues. Utilization of wood cellulose offer a great potential for increasing the use of lower-value biomass resources and reducing the raw material cost ([Fang et al., 2013](#_bookmark29); [Sirviö,](#_bookmark57) [Liimatainen, Niinimäki, & Hormi, 2013](#_bookmark57)). However, wood pulp is more

Recently, a system based on alkali/urea (7 wt% NaOH/12 wt% urea) aqueous solution has been developed to dissolve cellulose at −12 °C to obtain a transparent cellulose solution. This green system has been adapted to dissolve wood cellulose in our previous work and base on this system, regenerated cellulose gels and cellulose composite nano-particles have been fabricated ([Cai & Zhang, 2006](#_bookmark21); [Cai & Zhang, 2005](#_bookmark20); [Cai et al., 2007](#_bookmark19); [Chang, Duan, Cai, & Zhang, 2010](#_bookmark22); [Chang, Peng, Zhang,](#_bookmark23) [& Pang, 2009](#_bookmark23); [Gong, Wang, & Chen, 2017](#_bookmark31)).

This work is the first to prepare green cellulose composite hydrogel from MTM and wood cellulose based on the NaOH/urea system. The composite gel morphology, structure and properties were studied by the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron micro-scopy (TEM), Fourier transform infrared spectra (FTIR) and tensile tests. The adsorption properties of composite hydrogels were in-vestigated by UV–vis spectroscopy using MB as a model. Different ad-sorption equation and models were applied for fitting the experimental data to understand the adsorption mechanisms and kinetics.

# Experiment section

- 1.  _Materials_

The cellulose sample (aspen cellulose, bleached kraft pulp, Alberta-Pacific Forest Industries Inc., AB, Canada) with an _α_\-cellulose content of more than 87% and some hemicellulose was used in this study. Its viscosity-average molecular weight (_M![](data:image/png;base64,)_) was measured at 25 ± 0.05 °C

by viscometry and calculated by \[![](data:image/png;base64,)\] _\=_ 3.72 _×_ 10 2_M![](data:image/png;base64,)_0.77 to be 80 × 104

Da ([Cai & Zhang, 2006](#_bookmark21)). Sulfuric acid solution (3 wt%) are prepared via dilution of concentrated sulfuric acid (Fish Scientific, Canada). The Na-montmorillonite (MMT) (industrial grade) with a cation exchange ca-pacity of 100 meq/100 g was purchased from Anji Fenghong mon-tmorillonite materials Co. Ltd, Zhejiang, China. The chemical formulae of MMT is Na0.33Si4Ca0.33 (AlMg)2(OH)2. Urea, NaOH, methyl blue, ethanol and other reagents were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich Canada Ltd. (Oakville, ON, Canada).

- 1.  _Acid hydrolysis of cellulose_

Aspen cellulose (3.0 g) were added into a beaker with diluted sul-furic acid aqueous solution (3 wt%, 100 g) and were hydrolyzed under continuous stirring at 80 °C for 4 h. After thorough washing with deionized water, the hydrolyzed cellulose sample was obtained. After hydrolysis, the cellulose pulp contained 95% cellulose and a few of hemicellulose. Its viscosity-average molecular weight (_M![](data:image/png;base64,)_) was mea-sured at 25 ± 0.05 °C by viscometry and calculated by

\[![](data:image/png;base64,)\] _\=_ 3.72 _×_ 10 2_M![](data:image/png;base64,)_0.77 to be 9.6 × 104 Da (DP = 592).

- 1.  _Preparation cellulose/montmorillonite composite hydrogel_

Firstly, 5 wt% sodium montmorillonite (MTM) aqueous solution was prepared by dispersing several amount MTM into deionized water. Cellulose was dissolved in an aqueous 7 wt% NaOH/ 12 wt% urea so-lution pre-cooled to −12 °C to form a 4 wt% transparent cellulose so-lutions by the cycle of frozen-thawed ([Cai & Zhang, 2005](#_bookmark20)). The above

cellulose solution was subjected to centrifugation at 5000 rpm for 15 min at 5 °C to remove air bubbles. And the non-dissolved fraction was about 0.2%. Then a certain amount of MTM aqueous solution was added into the cellulose solution and mixed by stirring. The cellulose/ MTM solution was subjected to centrifugation at 5000 rpm for 15 min at 5 °C to remove air bubbles. The resultant MTM/cellulose solutions were spread on glass plate as 0.5 mm-thick layer and coagulated by non-solvent solution to give cellulose/MTM gels. After thorough washing with deionized water, the hydrogels were obtained. The cellulose/MTM hydrogels prepared from MTM with the concentration of 5 wt%, 10 wt

%, 20 wt% compared to cellulose were coded as CCH-5, CCH-10 and CCH-20, respectively. The aerogel samples for SEM and FTIR were prepared by freeze-drying.

- 1.  _Characterization_

The hydrogel samples were frozen in liquid nitrogen, and im-mediately snapped to expose the inner part. Then the samples were freeze-dried. The dried sample intersection morphology observation was carried out on a field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM, Zeiss-Sigma) by using an accelerating voltage of 5 kV. The sam-ples were coated with Pt for the SEM observation. Transmission elec-tron microscopy (TEM) images were observed on a JEOL JEM-2010 (HT) electron microscope, using an accelerating voltage of 200 kV. A copper grid coated with a holey carbon support film was used for prepare samples for TEM observation. A small piece of the central part of the result specimen was embedded in acetone and then to a 7:3 (v/v) mixture of methylmethacrylate and butylmehtacrylate monomers con-taining 1.4% (w/v) benzoyl peroxide as initiator at 25 °C for 6 h. Then ultrathin sections were prepared in an ultramicrotome equipped with a cryosectioning unit and the section approximately 100 nm thick was mounted on a grid with carbon support ([Manabe, Yokota, Minami,](#_bookmark50) [Uegomori, & Komoto, 2002](#_bookmark50)). The cellulose/MTM crystalline structure and interaction in the composite gels were studied with an FTIR (Perkin Elmer Spectrum one, Wellesley, MA, USA) spectrophotometer in the region of 400–4000 cm−1. The freeze-dried gels were analyzed in KBr

chemical skeleton of cellulose as the major adsorptions remained un-changed. The peak at 3300–3500 cm−1 was corresponded to the char-acteristic stretching vibration of hydroxyl groups. This peak became narrow in the cellulose/MTM composite hydrogel, indicating a strong hydrogen bonding interaction between cellulose and MTM. In the curves of CCH-10 and CCH-20, the appearance of the peak at 840 cm−1 corresponding to the vibration of Al-O-C, indicates the formation of Al-cellulose bonds via the hydroxyl group of the cellulose interacting with the Al on the MTM surface ([Liu, Walther, Ikkala, Belova, & Berglund,](#_bookmark47) [2011](#_bookmark47); [Wang et al., 2015](#_bookmark60)). It is likely these interactions enabled good distribution of MTM in the cellulose solution based on the NaOH/urea system, thus then led to formation of gels with intercalated phases well distributed in the gel networks. Fig. S3 shows the typical compression stress-strain curves of CH, CCH-5, CCH-10 and CCH-20. The compres-sive strength of the regenerated cellulose hydrogel is 3.5 MPa, and this value increased to 5.1 MPa for CCH-10. It could be explained by stronger interfacial interaction between cellulose and MMT. It is pos-sible that the stress transfer was facilitated by hydrogen bonding and Al-cellulose bonding between MTM sheet and cellulose.

- 1.  _The dye adsorption of cellulose/MTM hydrogel_

The time dependent UV-vis spectra of the MB dye solution after MB adsorption by cellulose hydrogel and cellulose/MTM composite hy-drogel (CCH-20) are shown in [Fig. 4](#_bookmark6). In [Fig. 4](#_bookmark6)a, the characterized ab-sorption peaks of MB dye were gradually weakened with the increase of the time, indicating the MB dye content decreased with the adsorption time. Moreover, photograms of cellulose hydrogel and cellulose/MTM hydrogel before and after adsorbing MB dye were shown in [Fig. 4](#_bookmark6)b. MB dye was almost removed from the solution by cellulose/MTM compo-site hydrogel, but not completely removed by the cellulose hydrogel alone, indicating the important role of MTM for MB dye adsorption in the composite gel.

The dye adsorption was further studied at three different MB con-centrations: 30, 80, 100 mg/L. The effect of initial concentration of dye on their removal by the cellulose/MTM composite gels are shown in [Fig. 5](#_bookmark7)(a–d). The adsorption capacity of cellulose/MTM composite hy-drogels was associated with the dye and MTM concentration. The ad-sorption capacity increased with the increasing concentration of MB dye. For example, the adsorption capacity of CCH-5 increased from 118 mg/g when the dye concentration increased to 176 mg/g from

30 mg/L to 100 mg/L. The highest adsorption capacity was observed for CCH-20 gel when the MTM concentration was 20 wt%, demonstrating a value of 277 mg/g at the concentration 100 mg/L of MB.

- 1.  _Adsorption kinetics_

For the liquid-solid adsorption system, the first order Lagergren equation (pseudo-first order equation) and pseudo-second order equa-tion have been applied to study the adsorption of pollutants from aqueous solution and they are related to the physisorption and che-misorption, respectively. These equations were used to fit the adsorp-tion date and the calculated kinetic parameters are represented in [Table 1](#_bookmark8). The first order kinetic model was more suitable for dye ad-sorption of cellulose/MMT hydrogel as reflected in the correlation coefficient value (R2) by the electrostatic interaction and hydrogen bond interaction. This suggests that the physisorption played most important role contributing to MB adsorption.

The intra-particular diffusion model could be used to analyze the diffusion mechanism. The kinetic results modeled by the intra-parti-cular diffusion model are shown in [Fig. 5](#_bookmark7)e and the calculated _Kp1_ and _Kp2_ are summarized in [Table 1](#_bookmark8). The _Kp1_ and _Kp2_ are ultra-particle dif-fusion rate constant of the first stage and the second stage adsorption, representing the external surface adsorption related to the boundary layer diffusion, and the intra-particle diffusion, respectively. The curve ([Fig. 5](#_bookmark7)) could be divided into three linear parts with different slopes attributing to the external surface adsorption, intra-particle diffusion and equilibrium stage. In [Table 1](#_bookmark8), according to the _Kp_ value, the ex-ternal surface adsorption stage was the fastest and the rate increased with the dye concentration. The second stage linear dependency did not pass through zero, suggesting that intra-particle diffusion was involved in the adsorption process, but was not the only rate controlling step ([Nesic, Velickovic, & Antonovic, 2012](#_bookmark52)). Moreover, the _Kp_ value of first stage (_Kp1_, boundary layer diffusion) was higher than the second stage (_Kp2_, intra-particle diffusion), suggesting that the second stage is the main rate controlling step. In addition, the adsorption process mainly occurred in the internal structure of composite hydrogel, indicating that the MTM well-dispersed in the composite gel matrix played the most critical role for MB dye adsorption.

- 1.  _Effect of pH_

The pH plays an important role in adsorption process and capacity. [Fig. 5](#_bookmark7)f shows the effect of pH on the MB dye adsorption. The dye ad-sorption capacity of the cellulose/MTM hydrogel increased with the increase of pH values and reached maximum at pH 7 (177, 205 and 254 mg/g for CCH-5, CCH-10 and CCH-20, respectively). In alkali condition, the dye adsorption capacity has decreased. It may be at-tributed to the decrease in removal tendency of oxides with the in-creasing of pH in the alkali condition. The exchangeable alkali and other metal ions on the surface and in the interlayer region of MTM undergo hydration creating a hydrophilic environment ([Lawrence,](#_bookmark42) [Kukkadapu, & Boyd, 1998](#_bookmark42)). Similar results were also observed for the adsorption of dyes on banana and orange peels ([Annadurai, Juang, &](#_bookmark14) [Lee, 2002](#_bookmark14)).

- 1.  _Effect of temperature_

The effect of the temperature on the adsorption of MB was in-vestigated at three different temperature (25, 40 and 50 °C) using the initial MB concentration of 100 mg/L. In Table S1, it can be seen that the adsorption capacity decreased with the MB solution temperature of CCH-10 and CCH-20. But the solution temperature had a slight effect on adsorption capacity of CCH-5.

- 1.  _Adsorption isotherms_

The adsorption isotherms of cellulose/MMT hydrogel were obtained by varying dye concentration from 30 to 100 mg/L. The Langmuir isotherm adsorption and Freundlich isotherm adsorption models were used to fit adsorption data. The Langmuir isotherm adsorption model assumes monolayer adsorption onto a surface containing a finite number of adsorption sites of uniform strategies with no transmigration of adsorbent in the plane surface ([Foo & Hameed, 2010](#_bookmark30)). The Freun-dlich isotherm describes the heterogeneous surface energies by multi-layer sorption ([Park et al., 2016](#_bookmark53)). As shown in [Table 2](#_bookmark9), the Freundlich equation was more suitable for adsorption isotherm than the Langmuir model according to the R2 value. The _n_ (empirical parameter) value related to the intensity of adsorption varies with the heterogeneity of the adsorbent. The parameter 1_/n_ indicates the intensity of adsorption and heterogeneity in a range between 0 and 1. The 1/_n_ data of Freundlich adsorption isotherm increased with MTM concentration and the result indicates that the composite hydrogel with higher content MTM was more uniform ([Dávila-Jiménez, Elizalde-González, & Peláez-Cid, 2005](#_bookmark26); [Nesic et al., 2012](#_bookmark52)). The results agree with the results of the gel structure observed by SEM and TEM. Moreover, the value of em-pirical parameter (_n_) was between 1–10, further supporting a good adsorption capacity of the composite hydrogels.

- 1.  _Comparison of the adsorption capacity and the possible interactions_

In [Table 3](#_bookmark10), the adsorption capacities of MTM composite hydrogel and MTM were exhibited. The results indicate the cellulose/MTM composite hydrogel has higher adsorption capacities than MTM alone. Moreover, composite hydrogel developed in this work exhibited the highest adsorption capacity (Qmax, 277 mg/g) at initial dye content of 100 mg/L. This is higher than many other natural material based ad-sorbents. For example, MTM alone showed the Qmax value of 245 mg/g at initial dye content of 700 mg/l; and chitosan/MTM showed the Qmax value of 55 mg/g at initial dye content of 400 mg/L. In accordance with the previous results, the adsorption capacities were improved with the increase of the content of MB dye.

The possible interactions between MB and cellulose/MTM hydrogel are shown in [Fig. 6](#_bookmark11). The MTM in composite hydrogel was negative charged ([Gürses et al., 2006](#_bookmark34)). The electrostatic interactions could be developed between the negative charged of adsorbent and the positive

charged of MB. Moreover, MB molecules were believed to be attracted to hydroxyl groups of cellulose hydrogel by formation of hydrogen bond ([Blackburn, 2004](#_bookmark18)). As shown in Fig. S4, the two significant bands decrease of the function groups were observed at the 3430 and 2916 which indicated th0065 –OH and C-H groups. These significant bands in the spectrum were involved the MB adsorption process. Nevertheless the kinetic study indicates that the physisorption played a more im-portant role for MB adsorption. Thus, it is likely that a larger number of adsorbates were adhered to the surface of MTM due to their large surface area when well-dispersed in the cellulose hydrogel matrix. As a raw materials, wood cellulose is a complex hierarchically structured organic material based on cellulose fibrils embedded in a matrix of hemicelluloses and lignin. Water solution is prone to permeate the non-crystalline portion of cellulose and all of the hemicellulose to facilitate MB penetration. Moreover, the wood-cellulose based matrix can bind MB molecules by functional groups such as carboxy, amino or phendics due to the existence of hemicellulose ([Demirbas, 2008](#_bookmark27)). These together may explain the excellent adsorption capacity observed for the cellu-lose/MTM composites hydrogels. Combination of the distinguishing feature of wood cellulose and MTM, the cellulose/MTM composite hydrogels have a potential application in the area of waste water treatment.

# Conclusion

In summary, here we reported a cellulose/MTM composite hydrogel that endows good adsorption capacity of methyl blue. Kinetic studies suggest that the physisorption was a major processing in the MB ab-sorption and the adsorption mainly occurred in the internal structure of composite hydrogel. These results suggest that most MB were adhered to the surface of MTM. The optimized composite hydrogels exhibited the highest adsorption capacity (_Qmax_, 277 mg/g) at initial dye content of 100 mg/L. Therefore the cellulose/MTM composite hydrogel have potentials to be used as an absorbent to treat colored organic effluent. Currently it is challenging to remove the dye adsorbed in the CCH. In the future, we will further improve the design to make the recyclable absorbent materials for economic reasons and environmental con-siderations.
